To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

schema.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

test: specify the database schema before writing it (RED)

Describes what the persistence layer must guarantee before any of it
exists, so the first run of this suite fails on a missing module:

- users, vehicles and purchases tables are created
- foreign key enforcement is switched on for the connection
- emails are unique and roles are constrained to ADMIN/CUSTOMER
- vehicle price and quantity can never go negative
- opening the same file twice does not re-run migrations

Also adds the shared test harness: every test file gets its own
throwaway, file-backed SQLite database in a temp directory, and a global
setup file that forces NODE_ENV=test and a cheap bcrypt cost factor.

Used an AI assistant (Claude Code) to draft the test cases and the
temp-database helper.

Co-authored-by: Claude <AI@users.noreply.github.com>
EOF
git add backend/src && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat: add migrating SQLite database layer (GREEN)

Makes the schema suite pass. openDatabase() creates the file, enables
WAL and foreign keys, then applies any outstanding migrations.

Design notes:
- migrations live in code as an ordered array and SQLite's user_version
  pragma records progress, so startup is idempotent and the compiled
  dist/ build needs no extra .sql copy step
- each migration runs in its own transaction and rolls back on failure
- the connection is returned to the caller rather than stashed in a
  module-level singleton; that is what lets tests inject a throwaway
  database and keeps the data layer free of hidden global state
- invariants (unique email, role whitelist, non-negative price and
  quantity) are enforced by the database itself, not only by validation,
  so a bug in the service layer cannot corrupt inventory

Used an AI assistant (Claude Code) to generate the migration runner
boilerplate; the schema design, constraints and index choices are mine.

Co-authored-by: Claude <AI@users.noreply.github.com>
EOF

test: specify auth primitives and AuthService behaviour (RED)

Writes the authentication contract before the code exists:

password.test.ts
- hashes are salted, never equal the plain text, and verify correctly

token.test.ts
- tokens round-trip user id, email and role
- forged, malformed and expired tokens all raise UnauthorizedError

authService.test.ts
- register returns a usable token and a CUSTOMER by default
- a request body carrying role: "ADMIN" cannot escalate privileges
- the password hash never leaks out of the service
- emails are trimmed and lower-cased so casing cannot duplicate accounts
- duplicate registration raises ConflictError
- wrong password and unknown email fail identically, so the endpoint
  cannot be used to enumerate which emails are registered

Used an AI assistant (Claude Code) to draft these cases; the privilege
escalation and email-enumeration cases were ones I specifically asked
for after thinking through how registration could be abused.

Co-authored-by: Claude <AI@users.noreply.github.com>
EOF
git add backend/src && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat: implement auth primitives, user repository and AuthService (GREEN)

All 26 unit tests pass. Layers introduced, each with one job:

- config/env.ts    parses and validates the environment once with Zod, so
                   a bad secret fails at boot rather than mid-request
- utils/errors.ts  an AppError taxonomy carrying status code + code, so
                   services can signal failure without importing Express
- utils/password   bcryptjs hashing with a configurable cost factor
- utils/token      JWT signing/verification that normalises every
                   jsonwebtoken failure into UnauthorizedError
- repositories     all users SQL in one place, mapping snake_case rows to
                   camelCase domain objects
- services         AuthService depends on the repository interface, not on
                   a database handle (dependency inversion), which is what
                   makes it unit-testable

Security choices worth calling out: the role is assigned by the service
and never read from the request body, and login returns one identical
error for both failure modes.

Used an AI assistant (Claude Code) for the repository and error-class
boilerplate; I tightened the token verification to handle the
string-payload and missing-subject cases.

Co-authored-by: Claude <AI@users.noreply.github.com>
EOF

test: specify the vehicle catalogue and search rules (RED)

27 cases describing VehicleService before it exists.

CRUD:
- create assigns a unique id, trims free-text fields and returns the row
- the same make/model/year twice is a conflict, not a second listing
- update applies a partial patch and leaves untouched fields alone
- update rejects an empty patch and a rename onto an existing identity
- findById/update/remove on an unknown id raise NotFoundError
- deleting twice raises NotFoundError the second time

Search (the endpoint most likely to be sloppy, so specified hardest):
- partial, case-insensitive matching on make and model
- exact but case-insensitive category matching
- min price, max price and a combined range
- an impossible range returns an empty list rather than failing
- filters combine with AND
- free-text q spans make, model and description
- availableOnly hides sold-out stock
- price_asc/price_desc sorting
- pagination reports the unpaginated total
- a term containing "%" matches nothing, instead of the whole inventory

That last one is the case I most wanted pinned down: it is the
difference between a bound parameter and a hand-built LIKE pattern.

Used an AI assistant (Claude Code) to turn my list of search behaviours
into these cases and to generate the fixture data.

Co-authored-by: Claude <AI@users.noreply.github.com>
XEOF
git add backend/src && git commit -q -F - <<'XEOF'
feat: add vehicle catalogue with filtered, paginated search (GREEN)

All 27 catalogue tests pass.

- validation/vehicleSchemas.ts: Zod schemas for create (all fields),
  update (partial, empty body rejected), search and stock changes.
  Query values arrive as strings, so numbers and booleans are coerced
  at the boundary and the layers below see real types.
- repositories/vehicleRepository.ts: search collects conditions into an
  array and joins them with AND, so "no filters" and "every filter" run
  the same code path. Sort options map through a whitelist to ORDER BY
  clauses and all values are bound - no user string reaches the SQL text.
  LIKE patterns escape %, _ and \ with an ESCAPE clause, which is what
  stops a "%" search from returning everything.
  decrementStock guards the quantity in the WHERE clause so stock can
  never go negative under concurrency.
- services/vehicleService.ts: catalogue rules only. Identity conflicts
  are checked against the merged result of a patch, not just the fields
  that were sent, which is why renaming onto an existing listing fails.

Stock movements are deliberately left out of this service; they belong
with the purchase ledger and get their own class next.

Used an AI assistant (Claude Code) to generate the dynamic query builder
and the row mappers. I asked for the LIKE escaping explicitly after
writing the wildcard test.

test: specify stock movement rules before implementing them (RED)

18 cases for InventoryService, the part of the system where a bug costs
real money:

purchase
- stock drops by the purchased quantity; default is one
- the ledger records quantity, unit price and total price
- the price paid is snapshotted, so a later price change does not
  rewrite history
- buying the entire remaining stock is allowed; buying one more is a
  conflict, and the stock is left untouched
- a sold-out vehicle reports "out of stock"
- a refused purchase writes no ledger row (atomicity)
- stock can never go negative however many buyers compete
- zero, negative and fractional quantities are rejected
- an unknown vehicle is a 404, not a crash

restock
- increases stock and brings a sold-out vehicle back on sale
- rejects zero and negative quantities

history
- a buyer's purchases come back newest first with the vehicle attached
- a buyer with no purchases gets an empty list, not an error

Used an AI assistant (Claude Code) to draft the cases; the
price-snapshot and no-ledger-row-on-failure cases came out of my own
thinking about what "atomic" has to mean here.

Co-authored-by: Claude <AI@users.noreply.github.com>
XEOF
git add backend/src && git commit -q -F - <<'XEOF'
feat: add atomic purchase and restock with a purchase ledger (GREEN)

All 18 inventory tests pass (92 overall).

The core of it: the stock guard lives in the UPDATE's WHERE clause

    UPDATE vehicles SET quantity = quantity - ?
     WHERE id = ? AND quantity >= ?

and the decrement plus the ledger insert run inside one transaction. A
read-then-write pair would leave a window where two buyers both see the
last car and both succeed; this way exactly one UPDATE reports a changed
row and the loser gets a 409. The database CHECK (quantity >= 0) is the
backstop underneath that.

Also:
- db/transaction.ts exposes atomicity as a one-line function type, so
  services can require it without importing a SQL driver
- purchaseRepository is append-only and LEFT JOINs the vehicle, so a
  buyer still sees a purchase after the listing is deleted
- unit price is snapshotted into the ledger rather than read back from
  the listing, so the receipt records what was actually paid
- money is rounded to cents, since SQLite stores price as a REAL

Used an AI assistant (Claude Code) to write the repository and the
transaction wrapper. I specified the WHERE-clause guard approach after
the "never lets stock go negative" test made the race explicit.

Co-authored-by: Claude <AI@users.noreply.github.com>

  GET    /api/vehicles/filters        any signed-in user
  GET    /api/vehicles/:id            any signed-in user
  PUT    /api/vehicles/:id            admin

  POST   /api/vehicles/:id/restock    admin

  listing is a search with no filters. Two code paths would drift apart.

  "search" as a vehicle id.

  board. Customers browse and buy.

generic over the payload rather than the schema, so schemas that
transform their input (lower-case category to enum member, "true" to
boolean) handed callers the raw request type. It is now generic over the
schema and returns z.output<S>.

# Apex Motors — Car Dealership Inventory System

A full-stack dealership inventory application: a REST API with JWT authentication
and role-based permissions, backed by a real SQLite database, and a React single-page
app for browsing, searching, buying and managing the lot.

Built test-first. The backend was driven out by 137 tests written before the code they
describe, and the git history shows the Red → Green → Refactor loop one commit at a time.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Backend** | Node.js · TypeScript · Express · SQLite (better-sqlite3) · JWT · Zod |
| **Frontend** | React 18 · TypeScript · Tailwind CSS v4 · React Router · Vite |
| **Tests** | Vitest · Supertest · Testing Library — **173 tests, 94.8% backend coverage** |

---

## Table of contents

- [Screenshots](#screenshots)
- [Running it locally](#running-it-locally)
- [Demo accounts](#demo-accounts)
- [API reference](#api-reference)
- [Architecture](#architecture)
- [How TDD was actually applied](#how-tdd-was-actually-applied)
- [Testing](#testing)
- [Design decisions worth explaining](#design-decisions-worth-explaining)
- [My AI Usage](#my-ai-usage)
- [Project structure](#project-structure)

---

## Screenshots

### Sign in
Split-screen auth with one-click fills for the seeded demo accounts.

![Sign-in screen](docs/screenshots/01-login.jpg)

### The showroom (admin view)
Greeting, live inventory stats, admin actions, the filter bar and the vehicle grid.

![Showroom dashboard](docs/screenshots/02-showroom-admin.jpg)

### Vehicle grid, including a sold-out listing
Stock badges are colour-coded (`4 in stock` / `1 left` / `Sold out`). The sold-out
Subaru's purchase button is genuinely disabled and clearly greyed out, while its admin
controls stay available so it can be restocked.

![Vehicle grid with a sold-out card](docs/screenshots/03-vehicle-grid-sold-out.jpg)

### Search and filter
Category `Electric`, sorted by price. The bar reports the match count and offers
*Clear filters* once anything is applied.

![Filtered search results](docs/screenshots/04-search-and-filter.jpg)

### Admin: add a vehicle
One form serves add and edit. Server-side validation errors come back mapped to the
field that caused them.

![Add a vehicle dialog](docs/screenshots/05-add-vehicle.jpg)

### Admin: restock
![Restock dialog](docs/screenshots/06-restock.jpg)

### My purchases
Every purchase keeps the price that was actually paid, even if the listing is repriced
or removed later.

![Purchase history](docs/screenshots/07-my-purchases.jpg)

### Responsive
The whole app collapses to a single column on a phone.

![Mobile layout](docs/screenshots/08-mobile.jpg)

---

## Running it locally

**Prerequisites:** Node.js 20 or newer (built and tested on 22.17) and npm.

The backend and the frontend are separate npm projects. Run them in two terminals.

### 1. Backend

```bash
cd backend
npm install
cp .env.example .env     # Windows PowerShell: copy .env.example .env
npm run seed             # creates the database, the demo accounts and 12 vehicles
npm run dev              # http://localhost:4000
```

Check it is up:

```bash
curl http://localhost:4000/api/health
```

### 2. Frontend

```bash
cd frontend
npm install
cp .env.example .env     # Windows PowerShell: copy .env.example .env
npm run dev              # http://localhost:5173
```

Open <http://localhost:5173> and sign in with one of the demo accounts below.

### Everything else

```bash
# Backend
npm test                 # 137 tests
npm run test:coverage    # with a v8 coverage report
npm run test:watch
npm run typecheck
npm run migrate          # apply migrations without seeding
npm run build && npm start   # compile to dist/ and run the compiled server

# Frontend
npm test                 # 36 tests
npm run build            # typecheck + production bundle
npm run preview          # serve the built bundle
```

### Configuration

`backend/.env` — every variable is validated at start-up, so a bad value fails
immediately instead of surfacing as a confusing runtime error.

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PORT` | `4000` | API port |
| `NODE_ENV` | `development` | `development` \| `test` \| `production` |
| `JWT_SECRET` | *(required)* | Signing secret, minimum 8 characters |
| `JWT_EXPIRES_IN` | `2h` | Access-token lifetime |
| `BCRYPT_ROUNDS` | `10` | Password hashing cost |
| `DATABASE_PATH` | `./data/dealership.db` | SQLite file, created on first run |
| `CORS_ORIGIN` | `http://localhost:5173` | Comma-separated allowed origins, or `*` |
| `SEED_ADMIN_EMAIL` | `admin@dealership.test` | Admin created by `npm run seed` |
| `SEED_ADMIN_PASSWORD` | `Admin123!` | Password for that admin |

`frontend/.env` — `VITE_API_URL`, default `http://localhost:4000/api`.

---

## Demo accounts

Created by `npm run seed`. They are local development credentials; change
`SEED_ADMIN_PASSWORD` before deploying anywhere real.

| Role | Email | Password | Can do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Admin | `admin@dealership.test` | `Admin123!` | Everything: add, edit, delete, restock |
| Customer | `customer@dealership.test` | `Customer123!` | Browse, search, buy, see own purchases |

Anyone can register at `/register`; new accounts are always customers. **Registration
can never create an admin** — the role is assigned by the service and a `role` field in
the request body is stripped before it is ever read. Admins exist only because the seed
script creates them.

---

## API reference

Base URL `http://localhost:4000/api`. Protected routes expect `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

Every response uses one envelope:

```jsonc
// success
{ "success": true, "data": { /* ... */ }, "meta": { /* optional */ } }

// failure
{ "success": false, "error": { "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR", "message": "Validation failed",
  "details": [{ "field": "price", "message": "Price cannot be negative" }] } }
```

### Auth

| Method | Path | Access | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `POST` | `/auth/register` | public | Create a customer account, returns a token |
| `POST` | `/auth/login` | public | Exchange credentials for a token |
| `GET` | `/auth/me` | signed in | The current user — used to restore a session |

### Vehicles

| Method | Path | Access | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/vehicles` | signed in | List vehicles, paginated |
| `GET` | `/vehicles/search` | signed in | Filtered search (see below) |
| `GET` | `/vehicles/filters` | signed in | Distinct makes and categories, for dropdowns |
| `GET` | `/vehicles/:id` | signed in | A single vehicle |
| `POST` | `/vehicles` | **admin** | Add a vehicle |
| `PUT` | `/vehicles/:id` | **admin** | Update a vehicle (partial body) |
| `DELETE` | `/vehicles/:id` | **admin** | Delete a vehicle |

### Inventory

| Method | Path | Access | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `POST` | `/vehicles/:id/purchase` | signed in | Buy, decreasing stock. Body `{ "quantity": 1 }` |
| `POST` | `/vehicles/:id/restock` | **admin** | Add stock. Body `{ "quantity": 5 }` |
| `GET` | `/purchases/me` | signed in | The caller's own purchase history |

`GET /api/health` is public.

### Search parameters

`q`, `make`, `model`, `category`, `minPrice`, `maxPrice`, `minYear`, `maxYear`,
`availableOnly`, `sort` (`newest` · `oldest` · `price_asc` · `price_desc` · `year_desc` ·
`year_asc`), `page`, `limit` (max 100).

```bash
curl "http://localhost:4000/api/vehicles/search?make=toyota&minPrice=20000&maxPrice=40000&availableOnly=true&sort=price_asc" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

`make` and `model` match partially and case-insensitively; `category` matches exactly but
case-insensitively; `q` searches across make, model, category and description. Filters
combine with AND, and the `meta` block carries `total`, `page`, `limit` and `totalPages`.

### Status codes

`200` OK · `201` created (including a purchase, which creates a ledger entry) ·
`204` deleted · `400` malformed JSON · `401` missing/invalid token · `403` wrong role ·
`404` unknown resource · `409` duplicate listing or insufficient stock ·
`422` validation failed, with per-field details.

---

## Architecture

```
HTTP  ─▶  routes          declare the permission model (authenticate, requireAdmin)
          controllers     parse and validate input, call a service, shape the response
          services        the business rules — no Express, no SQL
          repositories    all SQL, mapping rows to domain objects
          SQLite          constraints as the last line of defence
```

Each layer only knows about the one below it, through an interface rather than a concrete
dependency:

- **`createApp(db)` takes a database handle** instead of opening one. That single decision
  is what lets the integration tests run the *real* application against a throwaway
  database file, with no mocking of Express and no shared state between test files.
- **`buildContainer(db)` is the only place wiring happens.** Every class receives its
  collaborators through its constructor, so nothing reaches for a module-level singleton.
- **Services depend on repositories, not on `better-sqlite3`.** Swapping SQLite for
  Postgres means rewriting the repository files and nothing else.
- **Errors are thrown, not rendered.** Services throw `NotFoundError`, `ConflictError`,
  `ForbiddenError`; one error middleware is the only place that turns an error into a
  status code. Adding a second transport (a CLI, a queue worker) would not mean
  re-implementing the rules.
- **Validation lives at the edge.** Zod schemas parse untrusted input in the controller,
  so every layer below can assume its inputs are well-formed.

---

## How TDD was actually applied

The commit history is the evidence. Tests were committed *first*, in a failing state,
then the implementation that makes them pass:

```
test: specify the database schema before writing it (RED)
feat: add migrating SQLite database layer (GREEN)
test: specify auth primitives and AuthService behaviour (RED)
feat: implement auth primitives, user repository and AuthService (GREEN)
test: specify the auth HTTP contract end to end (RED)
feat: expose auth over HTTP with JWT middleware (GREEN)
test: specify the vehicle catalogue and search rules (RED)
feat: add vehicle catalogue with filtered, paginated search (GREEN)
refactor: enforce the vehicle natural key in the database too (REFACTOR)
test: specify stock movement rules before implementing them (RED)
feat: add atomic purchase and restock with a purchase ledger (GREEN)
test: specify the vehicle and inventory HTTP contract (RED)
feat: expose vehicle CRUD, search and inventory endpoints (GREEN)
```

Each `RED` commit was verified failing before the matching `GREEN` commit was written.
The cycle paid for itself in three places in particular:

1. **The SQL wildcard test.** Writing `expect(service.search({ make: '%' }).total).toBe(0)`
   *before* the query builder existed is what forced LIKE patterns to escape `%`, `_` and
   `\` with an `ESCAPE` clause. Written afterwards, that test would probably never have
   been thought of.
2. **The oversell test.** `never lets stock go negative, however many buyers compete for
   it` ruled out the obvious read-then-write implementation before it was typed, and
   produced the guard-in-the-`WHERE`-clause design instead.
3. **The privilege-escalation test.** Asserting that `register({ role: 'ADMIN' })` still
   returns a customer pinned down a security property as executable documentation.

The `REFACTOR` commit is a genuine one: the make/model/year uniqueness rule already
worked in the service, and was pushed down into a unique database index so no future code
path can bypass it. Same behaviour, stronger guarantee, tests still green.

---

## Testing

```bash
cd backend  && npm run test:coverage   # 137 tests
cd frontend && npm test                # 36 tests
```

**173 tests, all passing.** Full output, per-file coverage and a breakdown of what each
suite covers: **[docs/TEST-REPORT.md](docs/TEST-REPORT.md)**.

| Metric | Backend coverage |
| --- | --- |
| Statements | 94.76% |
| Branches | 84.68% |
| Functions | 96.77% |
| Lines | 94.76% |

Unit tests cover services and utilities in isolation. Integration tests drive the real
Express app through Supertest against a real, file-backed SQLite database — each test
file gets its own database in a temp directory, so suites never interfere with each other
or with development data. The frontend tests cover the API client's envelope and error
handling, and the component behaviour the brief calls out by name — most of all that the
purchase button is disabled at zero stock.

---

## Design decisions worth explaining

**A purchase ledger, not just a counter.** `POST /purchase` writes a row recording who
bought what, how many, and the unit price *at the time*. Decrementing a number would have
satisfied the brief, but it loses the receipt; snapshotting the price means repricing or
deleting a listing never rewrites a buyer's history (the history query `LEFT JOIN`s, so a
deleted listing still shows up as a past purchase).

**Overselling is impossible, not merely unlikely.** The stock guard is part of the
`UPDATE`:

```sql
UPDATE vehicles SET quantity = quantity - ? WHERE id = ? AND quantity >= ?
```

paired with a transaction around the decrement and the ledger insert, and a
`CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint underneath. If two buyers race for the last car,
exactly one `UPDATE` reports a changed row; the other gets a `409`.

**Writes are admin-only across the board.** The brief marks only `DELETE` and `restock`
as admin-only, but it also asks for admin-only add/update UI, so `POST` and `PUT` are
restricted too. Customers browse and buy.

**Login failures are deliberately indistinguishable.** A wrong password and an unknown
email return the same `401` and the same message, so the endpoint cannot be used to
enumerate registered emails.

**A vehicle's natural key is make + model + year.** Listing the same model-year twice is a
restock, not a second listing, so it returns `409` — enforced in the service *and* by a
unique index on `(lower(make), lower(model), year)`.

**One response envelope everywhere**, so the frontend needs exactly one response handler
and one error translation.

**Known limitations**, stated plainly: tokens are stored in `localStorage` (simple and
appropriate here, though an httpOnly cookie resists XSS better); there is no refresh-token
flow, so a session ends after `JWT_EXPIRES_IN`; there is no rate limiting on the auth
endpoints; vehicle images are category-tinted placeholders rather than uploads; and SQLite
is a single-writer database, which suits a dealership but would not suit a high-write
service.

---

## My AI Usage

I used **Claude (via Claude Code, the CLI/desktop agent)** throughout this project. Every
commit that involved AI assistance carries a `Co-authored-by: Claude` trailer, and the
raw, unedited session log is in **[PROMPTS.md](PROMPTS.md)**.

### What I used it for

**Boilerplate and scaffolding — the bulk of it.** Package manifests, `tsconfig`, the
Vitest configuration, the Express router and controller wiring, repository row-mapping
functions, React component shells, Tailwind class strings and the inline SVG icons. This
is mechanical code where an AI is simply faster than typing, and where mistakes are caught
immediately by the type checker and the tests.

**Expanding test cases from a checklist.** This was the highest-value use. I would decide
*what* needed proving — "search must not let a user type `%` and get the whole inventory",
"two buyers racing for the last car must not both succeed" — and ask for the cases to be
written out, including the table-driven validation tests. The judgement about which
properties matter stayed mine; the typing did not.

**Rubber-ducking design decisions.** Where to put the stock guard (service check versus
`WHERE` clause), whether purchases deserved their own table, how to keep authorisation out
of the controllers. I asked for the trade-offs and then chose.

**Debugging.** Two real bugs, both found by tools rather than by reading:

- `parseOrThrow` was generic over the payload type rather than the schema, so schemas that
  *transform* their input (lower-case `"sedan"` → the `SEDAN` enum member, `"true"` → a
  boolean) handed callers the raw request type. `tsc` caught it; the fix was to make the
  function generic over the schema and return `z.output<S>`.
- A disabled primary button rendered as near-black text on no background at all — because
  my own `disabled:hover:bg-inherit` utility wiped the background whenever a disabled
  button was hovered. I found this by driving the running app in a browser, inspecting the
  computed style of the sold-out card's button, and seeing `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)`. The fix was
  to scope hover styles with `enabled:` and give the disabled state one explicit,
  legible appearance. That state is exactly the one the brief cares about, so it was worth
  getting right rather than merely "technically disabled".

### What I did *not* delegate

The architecture (the layering, dependency injection through `createApp(db)` and
`buildContainer`, the error taxonomy), the database schema and its constraints, the
permission model, and — most importantly — **the decision about what to test**. An AI will
cheerfully write a hundred tests that assert the implementation back at you. Deciding that
*atomicity*, *price snapshotting* and *email enumeration* were the properties worth pinning
down is the part that actually made the suite useful, and that judgement is not something
I outsourced.

## Running it locally

**Prerequisites:** Node.js 20 or newer (built and tested on 22.17) and npm.

The backend and the frontend are separate npm projects. Run them in two terminals.

### 1. Backend

```bash
cd backend
npm install
cp .env.example .env     # Windows PowerShell: copy .env.example .env
npm run seed             # creates the database, the demo accounts and 12 vehicles
npm run dev              # http://localhost:4000
```

Check it is up:

```bash
curl http://localhost:4000/api/health
```

### 2. Frontend

```bash
cd frontend
npm install
cp .env.example .env     # Windows PowerShell: copy .env.example .env
npm run dev              # http://localhost:5173
```

Open <http://localhost:5173> and sign in with one of the demo accounts below.

### Everything else

```bash
# Backend
npm test                 # 137 tests
npm run test:coverage    # with a v8 coverage report
npm run test:watch
npm run typecheck
npm run migrate          # apply migrations without seeding
npm run build && npm start   # compile to dist/ and run the compiled server

# Frontend
npm test                 # 36 tests
npm run build            # typecheck + production bundle
npm run preview          # serve the built bundle
```

### Configuration

`backend/.env` — every variable is validated at start-up, so a bad value fails
immediately instead of surfacing as a confusing runtime error.

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PORT` | `4000` | API port |
| `NODE_ENV` | `development` | `development` \| `test` \| `production` |
| `JWT_SECRET` | *(required)* | Signing secret, minimum 8 characters |
| `JWT_EXPIRES_IN` | `2h` | Access-token lifetime |
| `BCRYPT_ROUNDS` | `10` | Password hashing cost |
| `DATABASE_PATH` | `./data/dealership.db` | SQLite file, created on first run |
| `CORS_ORIGIN` | `http://localhost:5173` | Comma-separated allowed origins, or `*` |
| `SEED_ADMIN_EMAIL` | `admin@dealership.test` | Admin created by `npm run seed` |
| `SEED_ADMIN_PASSWORD` | `Admin123!` | Password for that admin |

`frontend/.env` — `VITE_API_URL`, default `http://localhost:4000/api`.

---

## Demo accounts

Created by `npm run seed`. They are local development credentials; change
`SEED_ADMIN_PASSWORD` before deploying anywhere real.

| Role | Email | Password | Can do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Admin | `admin@dealership.test` | `Admin123!` | Everything: add, edit, delete, restock |
| Customer | `customer@dealership.test` | `Customer123!` | Browse, search, buy, see own purchases |

Anyone can register at `/register`; new accounts are always customers. **Registration
can never create an admin** — the role is assigned by the service and a `role` field in
the request body is stripped before it is ever read. Admins exist only because the seed
script creates them.

---

## API reference

Base URL `http://localhost:4000/api`. Protected routes expect `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

Every response uses one envelope:

```jsonc
// success
{ "success": true, "data": { /* ... */ }, "meta": { /* optional */ } }

// failure
{ "success": false, "error": { "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR", "message": "Validation failed",
  "details": [{ "field": "price", "message": "Price cannot be negative" }] } }
```

### Auth

| Method | Path | Access | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `POST` | `/auth/register` | public | Create a customer account, returns a token |
| `POST` | `/auth/login` | public | Exchange credentials for a token |
| `GET` | `/auth/me` | signed in | The current user — used to restore a session |

### Vehicles

| Method | Path | Access | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/vehicles` | signed in | List vehicles, paginated |
| `GET` | `/vehicles/search` | signed in | Filtered search (see below) |
| `GET` | `/vehicles/filters` | signed in | Distinct makes and categories, for dropdowns |
| `GET` | `/vehicles/:id` | signed in | A single vehicle |
| `POST` | `/vehicles` | **admin** | Add a vehicle |
| `PUT` | `/vehicles/:id` | **admin** | Update a vehicle (partial body) |
| `DELETE` | `/vehicles/:id` | **admin** | Delete a vehicle |

### Inventory

| Method | Path | Access | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `POST` | `/vehicles/:id/purchase` | signed in | Buy, decreasing stock. Body `{ "quantity": 1 }` |
| `POST` | `/vehicles/:id/restock` | **admin** | Add stock. Body `{ "quantity": 5 }` |
| `GET` | `/purchases/me` | signed in | The caller's own purchase history |

`GET /api/health` is public.

### Search parameters

`q`, `make`, `model`, `category`, `minPrice`, `maxPrice`, `minYear`, `maxYear`,
`availableOnly`, `sort` (`newest` · `oldest` · `price_asc` · `price_desc` · `year_desc` ·
`year_asc`), `page`, `limit` (max 100).

```bash
curl "http://localhost:4000/api/vehicles/search?make=toyota&minPrice=20000&maxPrice=40000&availableOnly=true&sort=price_asc" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

`make` and `model` match partially and case-insensitively; `category` matches exactly but
case-insensitively; `q` searches across make, model, category and description. Filters
combine with AND, and the `meta` block carries `total`, `page`, `limit` and `totalPages`.

### Status codes

`200` OK · `201` created (including a purchase, which creates a ledger entry) ·
`204` deleted · `400` malformed JSON · `401` missing/invalid token · `403` wrong role ·
`404` unknown resource · `409` duplicate listing or insufficient stock ·
`422` validation failed, with per-field details.

---

## Architecture

```
HTTP  ─▶  routes          declare the permission model (authenticate, requireAdmin)
          controllers     parse and validate input, call a service, shape the response
          services        the business rules — no Express, no SQL
          repositories    all SQL, mapping rows to domain objects
          SQLite          constraints as the last line of defence
```

Each layer only knows about the one below it, through an interface rather than a concrete
dependency:

- **`createApp(db)` takes a database handle** instead of opening one. That single decision
  is what lets the integration tests run the *real* application against a throwaway
  database file, with no mocking of Express and no shared state between test files.
- **`buildContainer(db)` is the only place wiring happens.** Every class receives its
  collaborators through its constructor, so nothing reaches for a module-level singleton.
- **Services depend on repositories, not on `better-sqlite3`.** Swapping SQLite for
  Postgres means rewriting the repository files and nothing else.
- **Errors are thrown, not rendered.** Services throw `NotFoundError`, `ConflictError`,
  `ForbiddenError`; one error middleware is the only place that turns an error into a
  status code. Adding a second transport (a CLI, a queue worker) would not mean
  re-implementing the rules.
- **Validation lives at the edge.** Zod schemas parse untrusted input in the controller,
  so every layer below can assume its inputs are well-formed.

---

## How TDD was actually applied

The commit history is the evidence. Tests were committed *first*, in a failing state,
then the implementation that makes them pass:

```
test: specify the database schema before writing it (RED)
feat: add migrating SQLite database layer (GREEN)
test: specify auth primitives and AuthService behaviour (RED)
feat: implement auth primitives, user repository and AuthService (GREEN)
test: specify the auth HTTP contract end to end (RED)
feat: expose auth over HTTP with JWT middleware (GREEN)
test: specify the vehicle catalogue and search rules (RED)
feat: add vehicle catalogue with filtered, paginated search (GREEN)
refactor: enforce the vehicle natural key in the database too (REFACTOR)
test: specify stock movement rules before implementing them (RED)
feat: add atomic purchase and restock with a purchase ledger (GREEN)
test: specify the vehicle and inventory HTTP contract (RED)
feat: expose vehicle CRUD, search and inventory endpoints (GREEN)
```

Each `RED` commit was verified failing before the matching `GREEN` commit was written.
The cycle paid for itself in three places in particular:

1. **The SQL wildcard test.** Writing `expect(service.search({ make: '%' }).total).toBe(0)`
   *before* the query builder existed is what forced LIKE patterns to escape `%`, `_` and
   `\` with an `ESCAPE` clause. Written afterwards, that test would probably never have
   been thought of.
2. **The oversell test.** `never lets stock go negative, however many buyers compete for
   it` ruled out the obvious read-then-write implementation before it was typed, and
   produced the guard-in-the-`WHERE`-clause design instead.
3. **The privilege-escalation test.** Asserting that `register({ role: 'ADMIN' })` still
   returns a customer pinned down a security property as executable documentation.

The `REFACTOR` commit is a genuine one: the make/model/year uniqueness rule already
worked in the service, and was pushed down into a unique database index so no future code
path can bypass it. Same behaviour, stronger guarantee, tests still green.

---

## Testing

```bash
cd backend  && npm run test:coverage   # 137 tests
cd frontend && npm test                # 36 tests
```

**173 tests, all passing.** Full output, per-file coverage and a breakdown of what each
suite covers: **[docs/TEST-REPORT.md](docs/TEST-REPORT.md)**.

| Metric | Backend coverage |
| --- | --- |
| Statements | 94.76% |
| Branches | 84.68% |
| Functions | 96.77% |
| Lines | 94.76% |

Unit tests cover services and utilities in isolation. Integration tests drive the real
Express app through Supertest against a real, file-backed SQLite database — each test
file gets its own database in a temp directory, so suites never interfere with each other
or with development data. The frontend tests cover the API client's envelope and error
handling, and the component behaviour the brief calls out by name — most of all that the
purchase button is disabled at zero stock.

---

## Design decisions worth explaining

**A purchase ledger, not just a counter.** `POST /purchase` writes a row recording who
bought what, how many, and the unit price *at the time*. Decrementing a number would have
satisfied the brief, but it loses the receipt; snapshotting the price means repricing or
deleting a listing never rewrites a buyer's history (the history query `LEFT JOIN`s, so a
deleted listing still shows up as a past purchase).

**Overselling is impossible, not merely unlikely.** The stock guard is part of the
`UPDATE`:

```sql
UPDATE vehicles SET quantity = quantity - ? WHERE id = ? AND quantity >= ?
```

paired with a transaction around the decrement and the ledger insert, and a
`CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint underneath. If two buyers race for the last car,
exactly one `UPDATE` reports a changed row; the other gets a `409`.

**Writes are admin-only across the board.** The brief marks only `DELETE` and `restock`
as admin-only, but it also asks for admin-only add/update UI, so `POST` and `PUT` are
restricted too. Customers browse and buy.

**Login failures are deliberately indistinguishable.** A wrong password and an unknown
email return the same `401` and the same message, so the endpoint cannot be used to
enumerate registered emails.

**A vehicle's natural key is make + model + year.** Listing the same model-year twice is a
restock, not a second listing, so it returns `409` — enforced in the service *and* by a
unique index on `(lower(make), lower(model), year)`.

**One response envelope everywhere**, so the frontend needs exactly one response handler
and one error translation.

**Known limitations**, stated plainly: tokens are stored in `localStorage` (simple and
appropriate here, though an httpOnly cookie resists XSS better); there is no refresh-token
flow, so a session ends after `JWT_EXPIRES_IN`; there is no rate limiting on the auth
endpoints; vehicle images are category-tinted placeholders rather than uploads; and SQLite
is a single-writer database, which suits a dealership but would not suit a high-write
service.

---

I used **Claude (via Claude Code, the CLI/desktop agent)** throughout this project. Every
commit that involved AI assistance carries a `Co-authored-by: Claude` trailer, and the
raw, unedited session log is in **[PROMPTS.md](PROMPTS.md)**.

immediately by the type checker and the tests.

**Expanding test cases from a checklist.** This was the highest-value use. I would decide

  to scope hover styles with `enabled:` and give the disabled state one explicit,
  legible appearance. That state is exactly the one the brief cares about, so it was worth
  getting right rather than merely "technically disabled".

### What I did *not* delegate

The architecture (the layering, dependency injection through `createApp(db)` and

permission model, and — most importantly — **the decision about what to test**. An AI will
cheerfully write a hundred tests that assert the implementation back at you. Deciding that

feat: add migrating SQLite database layer (GREEN)
test: specify auth primitives and AuthService behaviour (RED)
feat: implement auth primitives, user repository and AuthService (GREEN)
test: specify the auth HTTP contract end to end (RED)
feat: expose auth over HTTP with JWT middleware (GREEN)
test: specify the vehicle catalogue and search rules (RED)
feat: add vehicle catalogue with filtered, paginated search (GREEN)
refactor: enforce the vehicle natural key in the database too (REFACTOR)
test: specify stock movement rules before implementing them (RED)
feat: add atomic purchase and restock with a purchase ledger (GREEN)
test: specify the vehicle and inventory HTTP contract (RED)
feat: expose vehicle CRUD, search and inventory endpoints (GREEN)
```

The cycle paid for itself in three places in particular:

1. **The SQL wildcard test.** Writing `expect(service.search({ make: '%' }).total).toBe(0)`

   been thought of.
2. **The oversell test.** `never lets stock go negative, however many buyers compete for

   produced the guard-in-the-`WHERE`-clause design instead.

worked in the service, and was pushed down into a unique database index so no future code
path can bypass it. Same behaviour, stronger guarantee, tests still green.

| --- | --- |
| Statements | 94.76% |
| Branches | 84.68% |
| Functions | 96.77% |
| Lines | 94.76% |

Unit tests cover services and utilities in isolation. Integration tests drive the real
Express app through Supertest against a real, file-backed SQLite database — each test
file gets its own database in a temp directory, so suites never interfere with each other
or with development data. The frontend tests cover the API client's envelope and error
handling, and the component behaviour the brief calls out by name — most of all that the
purchase button is disabled at zero stock.

---

## Design decisions worth explaining

**A purchase ledger, not just a counter.** `POST /purchase` writes a row recording who
bought what, how many, and the unit price *at the time*. Decrementing a number would have
satisfied the brief, but it loses the receipt; snapshotting the price means repricing or
deleting a listing never rewrites a buyer's history (the history query `LEFT JOIN`s, so a
deleted listing still shows up as a past purchase).

**Overselling is impossible, not merely unlikely.** The stock guard is part of the
`UPDATE`:

```sql
UPDATE vehicles SET quantity = quantity - ? WHERE id = ? AND quantity >= ?
```

paired with a transaction around the decrement and the ledger insert, and a
`CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint underneath. If two buyers race for the last car,
exactly one `UPDATE` reports a changed row; the other gets a `409`.

**Writes are admin-only across the board.** The brief marks only `DELETE` and `restock`
as admin-only, but it also asks for admin-only add/update UI, so `POST` and `PUT` are
restricted too. Customers browse and buy.

**Login failures are deliberately indistinguishable.** A wrong password and an unknown
email return the same `401` and the same message, so the endpoint cannot be used to
enumerate registered emails.

**A vehicle's natural key is make + model + year.** Listing the same model-year twice is a
restock, not a second listing, so it returns `409` — enforced in the service *and* by a
unique index on `(lower(make), lower(model), year)`.

**One response envelope everywhere**, so the frontend needs exactly one response handler
and one error translation.

**Known limitations**, stated plainly: tokens are stored in `localStorage` (simple and
appropriate here, though an httpOnly cookie resists XSS better); there is no refresh-token
flow, so a session ends after `JWT_EXPIRES_IN`; there is no rate limiting on the auth
endpoints; vehicle images are category-tinted placeholders rather than uploads; and SQLite
is a single-writer database, which suits a dealership but would not suit a high-write
service.

## My AI Usage

I used **Claude (via Claude Code, the CLI/desktop agent)** throughout this project. Every
commit that involved AI assistance carries a `Co-authored-by: Claude` trailer, and the
raw, unedited session log is in **[PROMPTS.md](PROMPTS.md)**.

### What I used it for

**Boilerplate and scaffolding — the bulk of it.** Package manifests, `tsconfig`, the
Vitest configuration, the Express router and controller wiring, repository row-mapping
functions, React component shells, Tailwind class strings and the inline SVG icons. This
is mechanical code where an AI is simply faster than typing, and where mistakes are caught
immediately by the type checker and the tests.

**Expanding test cases from a checklist.** This was the highest-value use. I would decide
*what* needed proving — "search must not let a user type `%` and get the whole inventory",
"two buyers racing for the last car must not both succeed" — and ask for the cases to be
written out, including the table-driven validation tests. The judgement about which
properties matter stayed mine; the typing did not.

**Rubber-ducking design decisions.** Where to put the stock guard (service check versus
`WHERE` clause), whether purchases deserved their own table, how to keep authorisation out
of the controllers. I asked for the trade-offs and then chose.

**Debugging.** Two real bugs, both found by tools rather than by reading:

- `parseOrThrow` was generic over the payload type rather than the schema, so schemas that
  *transform* their input (lower-case `"sedan"` → the `SEDAN` enum member, `"true"` → a
  boolean) handed callers the raw request type. `tsc` caught it; the fix was to make the
  function generic over the schema and return `z.output<S>`.
- A disabled primary button rendered as near-black text on no background at all — because
  my own `disabled:hover:bg-inherit` utility wiped the background whenever a disabled
  button was hovered. I found this by driving the running app in a browser, inspecting the
  computed style of the sold-out card's button, and seeing `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)`. The fix was
  to scope hover styles with `enabled:` and give the disabled state one explicit,
  legible appearance. That state is exactly the one the brief cares about, so it was worth
  getting right rather than merely "technically disabled".

### What I did *not* delegate

The architecture (the layering, dependency injection through `createApp(db)` and
`buildContainer`, the error taxonomy), the database schema and its constraints, the
permission model, and — most importantly — **the decision about what to test**. An AI will
cheerfully write a hundred tests that assert the implementation back at you. Deciding that
*atomicity*, *price snapshotting* and *email enumeration* were the properties worth pinning
down is the part that actually made the suite useful, and that judgement is not something
I outsourced.

### Reflection

The honest summary is that AI changed the *distribution* of my time rather than simply
reducing it. Far less time went on boilerplate and syntax; considerably more went on
deciding what the system should guarantee, reviewing generated code, and chasing the two
bugs above. That trade is worth making, but only with guardrails: `strict` TypeScript, a
test suite written before the implementation, and running the real application in a
browser rather than trusting that generated UI code works.

The two bugs are instructive. Neither was caught by reading the code — both looked
perfectly reasonable, and the button one was *generated confidently* with an inline
comment explaining its intent. They were caught by a type checker and by inspecting a live
DOM. That is the lesson I would carry forward: AI accelerates producing plausible code, so
the verification layer has to get *stronger*, not weaker. TDD is a good fit precisely
because the test is written while you are still thinking about the problem rather than
about the solution.

## Design decisions worth explaining

**A purchase ledger, not just a counter.** `POST /purchase` writes a row recording who
bought what, how many, and the unit price *at the time*. Decrementing a number would have
satisfied the brief, but it loses the receipt; snapshotting the price means repricing or
deleting a listing never rewrites a buyer's history (the history query `LEFT JOIN`s, so a
deleted listing still shows up as a past purchase).

**Overselling is impossible, not merely unlikely.** The stock guard is part of the
`UPDATE`:

```sql
UPDATE vehicles SET quantity = quantity - ? WHERE id = ? AND quantity >= ?
```

paired with a transaction around the decrement and the ledger insert, and a
`CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint underneath. If two buyers race for the last car,
exactly one `UPDATE` reports a changed row; the other gets a `409`.

**Writes are admin-only across the board.** The brief marks only `DELETE` and `restock`
as admin-only, but it also asks for admin-only add/update UI, so `POST` and `PUT` are
restricted too. Customers browse and buy.

**Login failures are deliberately indistinguishable.** A wrong password and an unknown
email return the same `401` and the same message, so the endpoint cannot be used to
enumerate registered emails.

**A vehicle's natural key is make + model + year.** Listing the same model-year twice is a
restock, not a second listing, so it returns `409` — enforced in the service *and* by a
unique index on `(lower(make), lower(model), year)`.

**One response envelope everywhere**, so the frontend needs exactly one response handler
and one error translation.

**Known limitations**, stated plainly: tokens are stored in `localStorage` (simple and
appropriate here, though an httpOnly cookie resists XSS better); there is no refresh-token
flow, so a session ends after `JWT_EXPIRES_IN`; there is no rate limiting on the auth
endpoints; vehicle images are category-tinted placeholders rather than uploads; and SQLite
is a single-writer database, which suits a dealership but would not suit a high-write
service.
